sections.heading: When Is Easter in Greece? Get the Date Right Before You Book

blocks.text: Updated: August 2026
Easter is one of the most important dates on the Greek calendar, yet it is also one of the easiest dates for international travelers to misunderstand.
The confusion begins with a simple assumption: if a traveler's home calendar says Easter falls on a particular Sunday, surely Greece celebrates Easter on the same weekend.
Sometimes it does.
Sometimes it does not.

Greece primarily follows the Orthodox Christian Easter calendar, and Orthodox Easter can fall on a different Sunday from Easter observed by Western Christian traditions. That difference matters far beyond religious terminology because a traveler who checks the wrong date can accidentally plan ferries, hotels, road journeys or sightseeing around a major Greek holiday without realizing it.
The solution is not complicated, but it requires changing the way you think about Easter dates.
Do not simply ask when “Easter” occurs in your home country.
Ask specifically:
When is Greek Orthodox Easter in the year I am traveling?
Then mark not only Easter Sunday but also Good Friday, Holy Saturday and Easter Monday, because those surrounding days form the practical calendar window that matters to a Greece itinerary.

sections.heading: Greek Easter Means Orthodox Easter

blocks.text: When Greeks refer to Easter, or Pascha, they are generally referring to Orthodox Easter.
The religious observance belongs to the Eastern Orthodox Christian tradition and represents the most important celebration of the Orthodox liturgical year.
For travelers, however, the immediate practical issue is the calendar.

Western Christian churches and Eastern Orthodox churches can calculate Easter using different calendar frameworks and ecclesiastical conventions. As a result, Orthodox Easter and Western Easter sometimes coincide and sometimes occur on separate Sundays.
This means a traveler's national holiday calendar cannot automatically be used to predict what will happen in Greece.

Someone from the United States, United Kingdom, France or another Western country may see Easter marked in March or April and assume the same weekend will carry Greece's principal Easter celebrations.
That assumption needs verification every year.

sections.heading: Why Does Greek Easter Sometimes Fall on a Different Date?

blocks.text: The full theological and astronomical history behind the Easter calculation is complex, and this travel-planning page does not need to become a religious-calendar dissertation.
The useful explanation is that Easter is not assigned to one fixed calendar date such as Christmas on December 25.

Its date is calculated according to ecclesiastical rules involving the spring equinox and lunar cycle, while the Orthodox Church traditionally uses a different calendar basis for determining Easter than most Western Christian churches.
That is why the two Easter Sundays can separate.
In some years, Greece celebrates Easter on exactly the same Sunday as Western churches.
In other years, Orthodox Easter occurs later.
For travelers, the important lesson is not memorizing the calculation.
It is understanding that Greek Easter must be checked independently for every travel year.
Once you know that, the most common planning error disappears.

sections.heading: Easter Sunday Is Only One Date in the Travel Window

blocks.text: Travelers often search for Easter Sunday, write the date into the itinerary and assume the calendar question has been solved.
It has not.
If you are traveling through Greece around Easter, several adjacent days deserve equal attention because the holiday builds through Holy Week and continues beyond Sunday.
The most useful sequence to mark is:

rows: Beginning of the final Holy Week period

blocks.text: This is intentionally a calendar table, not an operational guide.
The dedicated Visiting Greece During Easter article owns what these dates mean for ferries, restaurants, opening arrangements and travel behavior.
Here, the objective is simply making sure those dates are visible before anything expensive becomes non-refundable.

sections.heading: Holy Week Moves With Easter Every Year

blocks.text: Because Easter Sunday changes, Holy Week changes with it.
There is no fixed annual date for Good Friday or Holy Saturday in Greece. They move backward from Easter Sunday each year.
This is important when travelers book trips months in advance.

Suppose your Greece vacation begins in mid-April. You may not think of it as an “Easter vacation” at all. Yet once the Orthodox Easter date for that particular year is checked, you might discover that Holy Saturday and Easter Sunday sit directly in the middle of your island itinerary.
The opposite can happen as well.
A traveler deliberately choosing Western Easter week may arrive expecting Greek Easter traditions and discover that Orthodox Easter is still several weeks away.
The calendar should therefore be checked before assigning cultural meaning to the dates.

sections.heading: Do Not Search “When Is Easter?” Without Adding Greece or Orthodox

blocks.text: Search engines can return the Easter date most relevant to the user's location, which is not necessarily the date observed in Greece.
The safer search behavior is specific.
Use terms such as:
Greek Orthodox Easter [year]
or
Easter in Greece [year]
rather than simply:
When is Easter?
This distinction seems minor until the wrong weekend affects a multi-stop itinerary.
Travelers planning a Greece journey six or twelve months in advance should record the Greek Orthodox date in the same document as their flight and hotel dates rather than relying on memory.
If Easter falls anywhere near the trip, the surrounding Holy Week dates should be added immediately.

sections.heading: Western Easter and Greek Easter Can Coincide

blocks.text: The fact that Orthodox and Western Easter sometimes differ can create another misconception: travelers assume they are always different.
They are not.
In some years, both traditions celebrate Easter on the same Sunday.

When that happens, international holiday travel and Greek domestic Easter activity can overlap more strongly, which may affect overall travel demand in ways that differ from years when the two calendars are separated.
From a planning perspective, this reinforces the need to check the actual year rather than using a general rule.
Never assume:
“Greek Easter is always one week later.”
It is not.
Never assume:
“Orthodox Easter is always in May.”
It is not.
The relationship changes.
The only reliable method is to verify the specific year.

sections.heading: Greek Easter Usually Falls in Spring, but That Is Still Too Broad for Planning

blocks.text: Travelers sometimes think that knowing Easter falls in spring is sufficient.
For weather packing, perhaps.
For transportation and accommodation planning, absolutely not.
A difference of even one or two weeks can affect whether the holiday overlaps with a particular hotel booking, ferry sector or mainland road journey.
It can also matter when the trip contains seasonal islands because spring is already a transitional period for tourism operations.
The useful planning unit is therefore the exact date, not simply March, April or May.
This is why Easter deserves its own calendar URL instead of being buried inside a general Best Time to Visit Greece article.
The seasonal page answers when Greece suits different travel styles.
This page answers one much narrower question: which dates are Easter dates?

sections.heading: Good Friday Is Two Days Before Orthodox Easter Sunday

blocks.text: This relationship is worth remembering because Good Friday is one of the dates travelers are most likely to encounter publicly.
If Greek Orthodox Easter Sunday is marked correctly, Good Friday can be identified immediately by moving back two calendar days.
The date matters because travelers may notice processions and increased religious activity that evening, but those cultural and operational implications belong to the Easter travel page.
For this URL, the useful knowledge is purely chronological:
Easter Sunday − 2 days = Good Friday.
This makes itinerary checking easier when a booking platform or calendar displays only Easter Sunday.
A traveler can quickly determine whether a planned Friday arrival or transfer coincides with the holiday period.

sections.heading: Holy Saturday Is the Night Before Easter Sunday

blocks.text: Holy Saturday often causes another calendar misunderstanding because one of the defining Easter experiences occurs at midnight.
The Resurrection celebration begins late on Saturday and reaches its central moment as the calendar turns into Easter Sunday.
Travelers who think only in terms of “Easter Sunday activities” may therefore overlook Saturday night entirely.
When reviewing travel dates, treat the evening before Easter Sunday as part of the principal Easter experience.
If your flight lands late on Holy Saturday, for example, you are arriving during a very different period from an ordinary Saturday night.
Again, the operational consequences belong to Visiting Greece During Easter.
This page's task is ensuring you recognize the date before the itinerary is finalized.

sections.heading: Easter Monday Still Belongs to the Holiday Calendar

blocks.text: International visitors often assume everything returns immediately to normal on Monday morning.
From a date-planning perspective, Easter Monday should still be marked as part of the holiday period.
It follows directly after Easter Sunday and remains relevant to travelers considering transportation, work schedules and the continuation of the Easter break.
The most cautious planning method is therefore not to circle one Sunday.
Create a visible Easter block running from at least Good Friday through Easter Monday, while recognizing that Holy Week begins earlier and the cultural atmosphere develops before Friday.
That simple calendar block makes later operational planning much easier.

sections.heading: Why the Exact Easter Date Matters More on a Multi-Stop Greece Trip

blocks.text: A traveler staying seven nights in one Athens hotel has relatively few moving parts.
A traveler combining Athens, Mykonos, Santorini and Crete has several.
Every hotel change and transport sector creates another date-sensitive component, which means Easter can intersect the journey in multiple ways.
Perhaps Good Friday occurs on the planned ferry day.
Perhaps Easter Sunday falls during Santorini.
Perhaps Easter Monday is the day scheduled for a regional flight.
Knowing the holiday dates early allows the itinerary to be reviewed before those services are booked.
This is especially important for Greek island journeys around Orthodox Easter, where the traveler is combining a moving religious holiday with a seasonal island network.
The date itself is the first piece of operational information.
Everything else follows from it.

sections.heading: When Should You Check the Easter Date?

blocks.text: Ideally, before choosing the final Greece travel dates if your journey falls anywhere within spring.
This is particularly important when:

items: travel occurs in March, April or early May,
the traveler expects an ordinary spring week,
or Easter traditions are one of the reasons for choosing Greece.

blocks.text: You do not need to redesign every spring holiday around Easter.
You simply need to know whether Easter is present.
There is an enormous difference between intentionally spending Easter in Greece and discovering after booking that your itinerary overlaps with it accidentally.
Awareness comes first.
Preference comes second.

sections.heading: When Should Easter Determine the Whole Trip?

blocks.text: Only when experiencing Greek Easter is one of the main travel goals.
If that is the case, start with Easter Sunday and build outward rather than fitting Easter into an already completed itinerary.
Decide where you want to be for Good Friday, Holy Saturday and Easter Sunday before committing to the surrounding route.
For Greece cultural trips timed around Easter, this calendar-first approach is more effective because the fixed holiday becomes the anchor and the rest of the itinerary can be positioned around it.
A traveler who does not care strongly about Easter should do the opposite: identify whether the holiday intersects the intended dates and then decide whether the overlap is acceptable.
Those are two completely different planning mindsets.

sections.heading: Do Not Treat Easter Date Calculators as an Itinerary

blocks.text: Knowing the date solves only the first problem.
It tells you when Greek Easter happens.
It does not tell you whether a ferry will be busy, whether a restaurant should be booked, whether Corfu suits your Easter trip or whether a museum operates with altered hours.
Those questions belong to another stage.
This separation is important both for travelers and for SEO architecture.
A page that answers every Easter-related question eventually becomes unfocused and competes with specialist content.
The clean sequence should be:

When Is Easter?
→ establish the dates.

Visiting Greece During Easter
→ understand how those dates affect the trip.

Destination pages
→ decide where in Greece you want to be.
That hierarchy creates a much stronger information cluster than one enormous Easter article trying to own everything.

sections.heading: Easter Dates Matter Even If You Are Not Religious

blocks.text: Travelers sometimes skip checking Easter because the holiday has no personal religious significance for them.
From a planning perspective, that is irrelevant.
National and cultural calendars affect travelers regardless of belief.

The same principle applies to Christmas, national holidays, festivals and major sporting events. You do not need to participate in the celebration for transportation demand, local routines or accommodation patterns to affect your trip.
Greek Easter deserves particular attention because it carries substantial cultural importance within Greece.
Checking the date is therefore practical travel preparation rather than religious planning.
You can decide afterward whether you want to participate in any Easter experiences at all.

It takes minutes.
It can influence decisions worth thousands of euros.

sections.heading: The Most Useful Easter Calendar Is Your Own Itinerary

blocks.text: Once the Greek Easter date is confirmed, stop thinking about it abstractly.
Place it directly into your actual travel sequence.
For example:

Wednesday: Athens
Thursday: Athens
Good Friday: Ferry / island
Holy Saturday: Island
Easter Sunday: Island
Easter Monday: Return journey
Now the effect becomes visible.
Perhaps that structure is exactly what you want.
Perhaps it makes you realize that one transfer should move by a day.
Either way, the Easter date has become planning information rather than trivia.
This is far more useful than simply knowing that Orthodox Easter occurs “later than usual” or “in April this year.”

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions About Greek Easter Dates
1. Is Greek Easter always later than Catholic or Protestant Easter?

blocks.text: No. Orthodox Easter can fall later than Western Easter, but the dates can also coincide. Travelers should verify the specific year rather than relying on a fixed assumption about how many days or weeks separate the two celebrations.

sections.heading: 2. Does Greece ever celebrate Easter in March?

blocks.text: Orthodox Easter can vary from year to year according to the ecclesiastical calendar calculation. Rather than relying on a general month rule, travelers should check the confirmed Orthodox Easter Sunday for the exact year of their Greece trip.

sections.heading: 3. How do I calculate Good Friday once I know Greek Easter Sunday?

blocks.text: Good Friday falls two days before Easter Sunday. Once the correct Greek Orthodox Easter Sunday has been identified, simply move back to Friday on the same calendar week to locate the corresponding Good Friday.

sections.heading: 4. Is Holy Saturday considered part of Easter weekend in Greece?

blocks.text: Yes, and it is particularly important because the Resurrection service takes place late on Holy Saturday leading into Easter Sunday. Travelers checking only Sunday may overlook one of the most significant calendar periods of the celebration.

sections.heading: 5. What date is Easter Monday in Greece?

blocks.text: Easter Monday is the day immediately following Greek Orthodox Easter Sunday. It should remain marked as part of the Easter holiday period when reviewing travel dates, even though the principal religious celebration centers on the preceding weekend.

sections.heading: 6. Can Greek Orthodox Easter fall in May?

blocks.text: Yes, depending on the year. This is one reason travelers planning late-April or early-May Greece trips should verify the Orthodox Easter calendar rather than assuming the Easter holiday has already passed.

sections.heading: 7. Is Palm Sunday the beginning of Greek Easter week?

blocks.text: Palm Sunday falls one week before Easter Sunday and leads into Holy Week. Travelers primarily concerned with logistics should focus particularly on the later part of Holy Week, although the religious calendar and atmosphere develop before Good Friday.

sections.heading: 8. Should I check Greek Easter even if I am visiting only Athens?

blocks.text: Yes. Athens is a year-round destination, but Orthodox Easter remains a major Greek holiday. Knowing whether your dates overlap allows you to review the relevant holiday information rather than unexpectedly encountering Easter-period schedules after arrival.

sections.heading: 9. Why does my phone calendar show a different Easter date from Greece?

blocks.text: Your calendar may be displaying the Western Christian Easter date commonly used in your country. Greece primarily observes Orthodox Easter, which can follow a different date, so travelers should search specifically for Greek Orthodox Easter for their travel year.

sections.heading: 10. If Orthodox and Western Easter are on the same date, which one does Greece celebrate?

blocks.text: Greece celebrates Orthodox Easter according to its religious tradition. When both calendars produce the same Sunday, the celebrations simply coincide rather than Greece switching to a Western Easter observance.

sections.heading: 11. How far in advance is the Greek Easter date known?

blocks.text: Easter dates can be determined well in advance, allowing travelers to incorporate them into future trip planning. If your Greece journey falls in spring, there is no reason to wait until shortly before departure to check whether Easter overlaps.

sections.heading: 12. What should I do immediately after confirming the Greek Easter date?

blocks.text: Place Good Friday, Holy Saturday, Easter Sunday and Easter Monday directly onto your planned itinerary. Then use the dedicated Easter travel guidance to review transportation, sightseeing and meal arrangements affected by the holiday rather than guessing from the date alone.

Orthodox Easter can vary from year to year according to the ecclesiastical calendar calculation. Rather than relying on a general month rule, travelers should check the confirmed Orthodox Easter Sunday for the exact year of their Greece trip.

3. How do I calculate Good Friday once I know Greek Easter Sunday?

Good Friday falls two days before Easter Sunday. Once the correct Greek Orthodox Easter Sunday has been identified, simply move back to Friday on the same calendar week to locate the corresponding Good Friday.

4. Is Holy Saturday considered part of Easter weekend in Greece?

Yes, and it is particularly important because the Resurrection service takes place late on Holy Saturday leading into Easter Sunday. Travelers checking only Sunday may overlook one of the most significant calendar periods of the celebration.

5. What date is Easter Monday in Greece?

Easter Monday is the day immediately following Greek Orthodox Easter Sunday. It should remain marked as part of the Easter holiday period when reviewing travel dates, even though the principal religious celebration centers on the preceding weekend.

6. Can Greek Orthodox Easter fall in May?

Yes, depending on the year. This is one reason travelers planning late-April or early-May Greece trips should verify the Orthodox Easter calendar rather than assuming the Easter holiday has already passed.

7. Is Palm Sunday the beginning of Greek Easter week?

Palm Sunday falls one week before Easter Sunday and leads into Holy Week. Travelers primarily concerned with logistics should focus particularly on the later part of Holy Week, although the religious calendar and atmosphere develop before Good Friday.

8. Should I check Greek Easter even if I am visiting only Athens?

Yes. Athens is a year-round destination, but Orthodox Easter remains a major Greek holiday. Knowing whether your dates overlap allows you to review the relevant holiday information rather than unexpectedly encountering Easter-period schedules after arrival.

9. Why does my phone calendar show a different Easter date from Greece?

Your calendar may be displaying the Western Christian Easter date commonly used in your country. Greece primarily observes Orthodox Easter, which can follow a different date, so travelers should search specifically for Greek Orthodox Easter for their travel year.

10. If Orthodox and Western Easter are on the same date, which one does Greece celebrate?

Greece celebrates Orthodox Easter according to its religious tradition. When both calendars produce the same Sunday, the celebrations simply coincide rather than Greece switching to a Western Easter observance.

11. How far in advance is the Greek Easter date known?

Easter dates can be determined well in advance, allowing travelers to incorporate them into future trip planning. If your Greece journey falls in spring, there is no reason to wait until shortly before departure to check whether Easter overlaps.

12. What should I do immediately after confirming the Greek Easter date?

Place Good Friday, Holy Saturday, Easter Sunday and Easter Monday directly onto your planned itinerary. Then use the dedicated Easter travel guidance to review transportation, sightseeing and meal arrangements affected by the holiday rather than guessing from the date alone.
